India’s AI Content Takedown Sparks Corporate Concerns!
India has notified tough amendments to the Information Technology Rules, 2021, set to take effect on 20 February 2026. 
Online platforms must  remove unlawful content within 3 hours of a government or court order!
#deepfake https://t.co/7ZcT35YazO

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

India just set one of the world’s tightest deadlines for deepfake moderation. 

As of February 20th, social platforms will have to remove AI-generated fakes and harmful synthetic content within 3 hours of a takedown order. 

Under these rules social platforms will have to deploy tools to verify those whether or not a piece of content is synthetic, and ensure that deepfakes are clearly labeled and embedded with traceable provenance data.

Platforms are going to need systems that can prove authenticity in real-time.

A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

Your Black Friday sales target is not your purchase order. 📦

One sets your ambition. The other commits your cash.

Miss the forecast: cash stays tied up in stock.
Beat it: replenishment may arrive too late.
Expedite it: freight eats into margin.

For supplement brands selling into the U.S., add expiration dates, subscription renewals, and shared bundle inventory.

Four questions to answer in October 👇

1️⃣ What happens on either side of the forecast?

Model conservative, expected, and upside demand for key SKUs. Check stock coverage, replenishment gaps, and leftovers.

Value remaining stock at cost. Separately map when deposits, balances, freight, and warehouse fees come due.

Review lots and expiration dates. Multipacks need enough shelf life for expected consumption and your customer promise. Confirm warehouse lot records and picking rules.

2️⃣ How much stock actually belongs to the promotion?

Subtract committed orders, unavailable units, and reserves for subscriptions and other channels before allocating promotional stock.

Check shared bundle components: one stockout could take several offers offline.

Align VIP early access, the main promotion, and existing customer demand in one allocation plan shared by marketing, purchasing, and fulfillment.

3️⃣ Does the offer still work after fulfillment costs?

Pack a complete sample: products, gift, insert, and box.

Use its weight, dimensions, picking fees, packing labor, and shipping costs to calculate contribution margin and allowable acquisition cost.

Our team can support labeling, custom packaging, kitting, inspection, and pre-packing before overseas shipment.

Document contents, packaging version, label placement, and pre-kit quantities. Keep stock flexible for single-unit orders and demand changes.

4️⃣ When will you act if sales deviate?

Plan through production, inspection, transit, receiving, and availability for fulfillment.

Our team can map these milestones and compare U.S. warehouse fulfillment with suitable China-direct options, after confirming product storage and shipping requirements.

Set triggers for:
→ Reordering or switching eligible shipping methods
→ Revising costs and customer delivery promises
→ Adjusting purchasing or kitting if demand slows

Confirm availability and fees for weekend processing, priority inspection, and expedited receiving.

📊 How much can you commit to stock—and when can you afford to scale?

Use the Shopify Black Friday Inventory & Scale Planning Worksheet to compare three demand scenarios, inventory gaps and leftovers, order economics, cash timing, replenishment milestones, and fulfillment contingencies.

🚨 #FACTCHECK: Nigel Farage on Burnham, Russia and Brexit

‘Mirror, mirror, on the wall, whose claims stand up after all?’

I’m a retired academic, media literate, and equipped with critical thinking skills, so I have time to do this quickly and accurately.

Earlier today, Nigel Farage called Prime Minister Andy Burnham “a liar” over his claim that Russia interfered in the 2016 EU referendum. Here is how Farage’s statements hold up against the record.

In an interview with The Rest Is Politics  podcast, released on 12 October but widely reported the day before, Burnham said that on taking office in July he asked whether Russia had interfered in the 2016 referendum, and was given “the clear answer that yes there was.” He did not say how Russia interfered and did not publish any evidence.

This morning, Farage held a press conference in Dover, Kent, to launch Reform UK’s asylum plans. LBC’s Emma Corr asked whether Burnham’s claim tainted the result, and how Farage felt about having potentially benefited from possible Russian interference. He later repeated several of his claims in an interview with GB News.

The exchange between Corr and Farage is available on YouTube from 1:00:07: https://t.co/zJMuAlHXdx

1. “The prime minister is a liar. Yes, a liar.”

Verdict: Unsupported.

Lying means knowingly saying something false. Burnham reported advice he says he received on entering No 10. That advice has not been made public, so his claim is unverified, and critics are entitled to say so. Nothing Farage cited shows that Burnham knew it to be untrue. At most, Farage offered evidence that the claim is unproven.

2. “Boris Johnson, when he became foreign secretary, one of the first questions he asked was, ‘Was there seen to be Russian interference in the referendum campaign?’ And the answer was no.”

Verdict: Misleading.

I could find no public record of this exchange. Johnson’s recorded public position was more qualified. In Moscow in December 2017, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said Johnson had confirmed Russia had not interfered in the referendum. Johnson interrupted him: “Not successfully.” He went on to say that Russian attempts to interfere in British elections and the referendum, whatever they may have been, had not succeeded. His position was that attempts may have been made and had failed, which is a different claim from “no”.

The premise that anyone checked is also doubtful. Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC) published its Russia Report in July 2020. It found that the government “had not seen or sought evidence of successful interference” in UK democratic processes. It called for an intelligence assessment of the referendum, and the government refused.

In 2019, BuzzFeed reported two anonymous sources saying British intelligence had found no evidence of Russian meddling in the referendum. That claim was unverified, and the ISC’s report the following year said the government had not sought such evidence.

3. Stephen Doughty “rowed it back and said even if there was some, it made no difference.”

Verdict: Misrepresents the minister.

Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, did narrow Burnham’s claim during Monday morning’s broadcast interviews. He told LBC that Russia had attempted to interfere in the vote but had not succeeded, and made the same point to Sky News. He also said Burnham had been making a broader point about Russian attempts to interfere in democratic events in the UK and across Europe.

On the @BBC Today programme, which Farage named, Doughty spoke of Russian attempts to interfere in a range of democratic processes. He cited the jailing of former Reform UK Wales leader Nathan Gill for taking bribes to promote pro-Kremlin narratives.

Farage’s summary distorts this. “Even if there was some” turns Doughty’s acknowledgement of attempts into a hypothetical. Farage followed it with the words “There was no Russian interference,” and in his later GB News interview (see 10) he attributed that denial to Doughty himself. I found no report of Doughty’s interviews containing those words, or anything to that effect. Doughty said Russia tried to interfere.

4. “There was no Russian interference… And the Russia hoax has run all the way through this.”

Verdict: Not supported by the evidence.

No official finding says there was no interference. The government’s position since 2020 has been narrower: “We have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU Referendum.” The ISC noted open-source studies pointing to anti-EU content on the Russian state outlets RT and Sputnik, and to the use of bots and trolls, as evidence of attempts to influence the campaign. It criticised the government for not investigating.

The defensible position is that attempts at influence were plausibly documented, their effect was never assessed, and no public evidence shows they changed the result. “No interference” and “hoax” both go well beyond that. The same standard applies to Burnham, whose “clear answer” rests on advice the public has not seen.

5. Arron Banks “was severely libelled over this. But in the end … [he] won in the high court.”

Verdict: False.

Banks sued the journalist Carole Cadwalladr over a 2019 TED Talk and a tweet. He lost in the High Court in June 2022, where the judge held that Cadwalladr’s public interest defence covered the talk. In February 2023, the Court of Appeal found partly in his favour, on one of his three grounds of appeal. It ruled that the defence lapsed for the talk’s continued publication after 29 April 2020, the date of an Electoral Commission statement clearing Banks. It upheld the dismissal of his claim over the tweet. Cadwalladr was ordered to pay £35,000 in damages and 60% of Banks’s High Court costs.

The case also had no bearing on whether Russia interfered in the referendum. It concerned Cadwalladr’s statement about Banks and “his covert relationship with the Russian Government.”

6. “I don’t think our growth figures are anything to write home about. But … they’re a damn sight better than France and Germany and Italy.”

Verdict: Accurate for this year, but selective over the longer term, and beside the point.

On current figures Farage has a case. In the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 0.5%, against 0.3% in Germany and zero in France. The IMF’s July forecasts put the UK third in the G7 for 2026, at 1%, behind the US (2.3%) and Canada (1.1%). That is ahead of Germany (0.7%), France and Japan (both 0.6%) and Italy (0.5%). The OECD’s September forecasts placed the UK joint second in the G7, level with Germany at 1.1%.

The longer view is less flattering. Between the end of 2019 and the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 6.2%, behind the eurozone as a whole (7.6%) and far behind the US (15.6%), though well ahead of Germany (1.9%, the lowest in the G7).

By naming France, Germany and Italy, Farage compared the UK with three of Europe’s weaker performers, while the eurozone overall has grown faster since the pandemic. Headline growth has also been flattered by rapid population growth. In late 2024, the Resolution Foundation found UK GDP per head still below its end-2019 level, although per-head growth picked up to 0.6% in the first quarter of 2026.

More importantly, none of these comparisons answers Burnham’s claim. Whether Brexit has done “more harm than good” depends on how the UK compares with a UK that stayed in the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) assumes Brexit will leave UK trade around 15% lower in the long run, and potential productivity around 4% lower, than if the UK had remained. In 2024 it said these assumptions appeared “broadly on track.”

Some economists, including Julian Jessop, a former chief economist and head of the Brexit unit at the free-market Institute of Economic Affairs, dispute these estimates.

Even so, the official forecaster’s central view is that Brexit carries a long-run cost, and growth rankings, whether flattering or not, do not settle the question.

7. “If you even look at trade numbers, the increase in trade since Brexit…”

Verdict: Partly accurate, but selective.

Total UK exports have grown since the referendum. Briefings for Britain, a pro-Brexit research group using ONS data, puts total exports in 2025 at 5% above 2019 in real terms. That growth has come from services. The House of Commons Library reports that UK services exports to the EU were 28% above their 2019 level in real terms in 2025. However, goods exports to the EU were 14% below it, having fallen in real terms in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Not all of that fall is due to Brexit, but post-Brexit barriers fall mainly on goods, and goods trade with the EU is where the decline shows. The overall total obscures it.

8. Brexit has brought “some level of inconvenience… showing a passport, filling in a form,” amounting to “mild inconveniences.”

Verdict: Understatement.

Farage conceded there was more inconvenience “for people like Alcaline,” a Kent road haulage firm based near Hythe, but described it as “showing a passport, filling in a form.” The evidence suggests that undersells the effect, particularly for firms moving goods across the Channel.

In March 2024 the OBR reported that UK goods trade was around 10% below 2019 levels and growing well behind other advanced economies, while services trade had grown more strongly than in the rest of the G7. The OBR attributed the gap partly to post-Brexit barriers falling mainly on goods.

Brexit is not the only cause of the 14% real-terms fall in goods exports to the EU, but official forecasters attribute part of it to post-Brexit trade barriers, which go well beyond passports and forms. Farage’s answer also merges two separate issues: control of migration, and the trade frictions that come from leaving the single market and customs union.

9. Burnham is “looking forward to sitting down with Marine Le Pen or the AfD”

Verdict: Speculation, contrary to the record.

Farage offered no basis for this. In the interview that prompted the row, Burnham cited the German chancellor’s view that the AfD were linked to, and possibly funded by, Russia. He presented the party as a threat to European democracy.

10. The GB News version

Verdict: False.

In an interview with GB News later that day, Farage said Doughty, “being interviewed on the BBC this morning, disavowed it and said no, there was no Russian interference, it didn’t affect anything.” The “even if there was some” qualification had gone, leaving a flat denial attributed to the minister. Doughty’s reported position was that Russia attempted to interfere but did not succeed, which confirms attempted interference.

Farage also presented Johnson and Doughty together as evidence that “both Labour and Conservative camps” reject Burnham’s claim. Neither man said there was no interference. Johnson’s recorded words in 2017 were “Not successfully.” Doughty said Russia had tried and failed. What both rejected was the narrower claim that interference succeeded, which is also the extent of the official government position since 2020.

Conclusion

Farage’s sharpest claims are his weakest. Nothing presented shows that Burnham lied.

Johnson’s record says “not successfully” rather than “no”. The minister Farage cited acknowledged Russian attempts. In Dover, Farage turned that acknowledgement into a hypothetical, and on GB News into a flat denial. Banks did not win in the High Court.

Farage is on firmer ground on recent growth rankings and on total exports, though neither settles whether Brexit has helped or harmed the UK, and goods trade with the EU tells a different story.

Burnham, for his part, has made a significant claim without publishing the evidence behind it. The assessment the ISC recommended six years ago would serve the public better than either man’s certainty.

Finally, it is worth measuring Farage by his own yardstick. Farage called the British prime minister a liar. 

The evidence he offered went only to whether Burnham was wrong, not to whether he knew it. If being wrong, or being unable to prove a claim, is enough to make someone a liar, the same test can be applied to Farage.

By that standard, his answer in Dover contained five “lies”: that Johnson was told there was no interference; that Doughty conceded only that any interference “made no difference”; that there was no Russian interference; that the affair was a “hoax”; and that Arron Banks “won in the high court.”

On GB News he added a sixth, that “both Labour and Conservative camps” deny any interference, and repeated three of the others.

That makes six distinct claims, and nine in all, across two appearances in a single day. The row began over one claim by Burnham.

The fairer test, and the one this fact check applies, is that lying requires knowing a statement to be false. By that measure, nobody can say Farage lied, any more than he can say it of Burnham.

But on the evidence, Burnham’s claim remains unproven, while at least one of Farage’s, about his friend’s libel case, is plainly false on the public record.

text:
Every week someone tells me they vibe-coded their app over the weekend and don't need developers anymore.

Before it touches a paying customer, make sure it includes:

> a schema someone designed, instead of one the AI improvised table by table
> login that still works when someone puts a plus sign in their email
> password reset links that expire and work once
> MFA, plus a recovery path for the user who lost their phone
> sessions that time out, and a way to kill every session for one user
> SSO for the enterprise customer who won't sign without it
> SAML, because that customer's IT team doesn't do magic links
> SCIM, so a fired employee loses access the moment IT offboards them
> roles and permissions deeper than "admin" and "everyone else"
> checks that stop user A from reading user B's data by changing one number in the URL
> tenant isolation, so one customer's bug never shows another customer's records
> an admin "log in as this user" button for support, with an audit trail on every use
> rate limits on login, so nobody can guess passwords at scale
> lockouts that stop attackers without locking out your CFO the night before the board meeting
> database migrations that run forward and roll back
> migrations that don't lock the main table at 2pm on a Tuesday
> indexes, because the query that was instant on 50 test rows times out on 5 million real ones
> connection pooling, so a traffic spike doesn't exhaust the database
> backups every night
> a restore from those backups, tested, because a backup you've never restored is a hope
> point-in-time recovery for the day someone runs a delete without a where clause
> soft deletes, so "I deleted it by accident" is a support ticket and not an incident
> validation on the server, not just in the form
> timezones stored right, so the 9am reminder doesn't fire at 4am
> the customer with an apostrophe in their last name
> emoji, accents and right-to-left text in every field
> money stored as integers, because 0.1 + 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3 in floating point
> currency, rounding and tax rules for every country you sell into
> a data model that survives your second customer asking for "one small change"
> idempotency keys, so a retried payment doesn't charge the card twice
> deduplication for the user who clicks submit four times
> pagination that still works on page 400
> exports, because sooner or later every customer wants their data in a spreadsheet
> imports that survive the CSV someone saved in 2009
> retention rules, and code that deletes what your contract says you'll delete
> secrets out of the code, out of the repo and out of the AI chat history
> rotating every key the AI pasted into a config file last month
> confirming every package the AI installed exists and is the one you meant
> dependency scanning, because the AI pulled in libraries nobody reviewed
> input sanitization everywhere a user can type
> protection against SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and the rest of the OWASP list
> file uploads that get scanned, size-limited and stored where they can't execute
> CORS rules that aren't "allow everything"
> security headers on every response
> encryption at rest and in transit
> least-privilege access for everyone, including the AI agent holding production credentials
> logs that record who did what, without recording passwords, tokens or card numbers
> a penetration test before your enterprise customer's security team runs their own
> answers to the security questionnaire every enterprise buyer sends, with evidence behind each one
> a disclosure process for the day a stranger emails you a vulnerability
> a plan for the day a laptop with production access gets stolen
> SOC 2, which means policies, evidence and an auditor, not a checkbox
> HIPAA, the moment a single patient record touches your system
> a BAA with every vendor that touches that data, including your AI model provider
> audit trails that show who viewed a record, not just who changed it
> PCI scope, and card numbers kept out of your database
> GDPR deletion requests that reach every table, backup and log
> data residency for the customer whose contract says EU only
> quarterly access reviews someone signs off on
> dev, staging and production environments that match each other
> infrastructure written as code, so the setup lives somewhere other than one person's memory
> a deploy pipeline that runs the tests before anything reaches customers
> one-click rollbacks, because Friday deploys happen
> zero-downtime deploys, because your customers don't have maintenance windows
> feature flags, so you can ship the code without shipping the feature
> autoscaling for the Monday morning spike
> a CDN, so the app loads fast in Singapore too
> DNS, SSL certificates, and renewals that don't expire on a Sunday
> background job queues, so slow work doesn't freeze the page
> retries with backoff, so one flaky API call doesn't become a lost order
> a dead-letter queue for the jobs that fail every retry
> cron jobs that don't run twice the day you add a second server
> caching, and clearing that cache when the data changes
> SPF, DKIM and DMARC, so your password resets don't land in spam
> bounce and complaint handling on every transactional email
> storage rules, so you stop paying to keep 2021's temp files
> cost alerts, so a runaway agent loop shows up the same day and not on the invoice (we learned this one for $1,382.59)
> a disaster recovery plan, written down and tested once a year
> a second region, if your contract promises uptime one region can't deliver
> structured logs you can search at 3am
> error tracking that groups the same bug instead of sending you 4,000 emails
> uptime checks from outside your own network
> alerts that page a human, tuned until they stop paging for nothing
> dashboards for latency, error rate and throughput
> tracing for one slow request across every service it touches
> an on-call rotation, and a person who picks up
> runbooks, so the engineer on call knows what "queue depth critical" means
> postmortems that change something
> a status page customers check before they email you
> unit tests written by someone who knows what the logic should do
> integration tests for every third-party API you depend on
> end-to-end tests for signup, checkout and the other flows that make you money
> load testing before the launch email goes out
> test data that looks like production without being production data
> regression tests, so fixing bug 41 doesn't bring back bug 12
> testing on the five-year-old laptop your biggest customer's ops team still uses
> accessibility compliance, because the enterprise contract requires it
> subscriptions, upgrades, downgrades and proration
> failed-payment retries and dunning emails
> invoices with the customer's PO number on them, because procurement won't pay without it
> sales tax and VAT
> refunds, credits and partial refunds
> usage metering that matches what you bill, to the cent
> annual contracts with custom terms your billing logic never planned for
> revenue reports your finance team can reconcile
> webhooks that verify signatures
> webhooks that retry, with a log of every failed delivery
> a versioned API, so you can change it without breaking your customers' integrations
> API keys customers can create and revoke
> API rate limits that protect you without blocking real integrations
> a plan for the day a third-party API changes its response format without telling you
> OAuth token refresh, because tokens expire at the worst possible moment
> a sandbox where customers can test their integration
> protection against prompt injection in every field that reaches the model
> customer and patient data kept out of prompts that leave your network
> a model spend cap per customer, so one heavy user can't run up your bill
> evals, so you find out when a model update makes your answers worse
> a fallback for the afternoon your model provider goes down
> a migration plan for the day your model gets deprecated
> prompt and output logs for debugging, minus whatever you're not allowed to keep
> a human approval step for anything the AI does that can't be undone
> pages that load on hotel wifi
> empty states, loading states and error states on every screen
> error messages a customer can act on, instead of "something went wrong"
> forms that keep what people typed when one field fails validation
> emails that render in every mail client your customers use
> notifications people can turn off
> undo
> keyboard navigation and screen reader support
> translations, with dates and numbers formatted for each locale
> a back button that does what people expect
> code a human can read
> code review on every change
> a branching strategy, so two people can work without overwriting each other
> monthly dependency upgrades, so you're never two major versions behind
> framework upgrades before the old version stops getting security patches
> deleting the dead code the AI left behind from its first three attempts
> splitting up the 2,000-line file the AI kept appending to
> architecture decisions written down, with the reasons
> a README that gets a new engineer running locally in under an hour
> documentation for whoever inherits this
> an admin panel for your ops team
> support tooling, so customer success can answer questions without pinging engineering
> a changelog customers can read
> terms and a privacy policy that match what the code does
> every account, domain and repo in the company's name, not the name of whoever built the prototype
> a bus factor higher than one

Oh, and besides keeping all of this working every day, forever… your vibe-coded app will still need people who know what they're doing:

> reading every line the AI wrote before it ships (a senior engineer)
> designing the data model before your second customer breaks it (a backend engineer)
> explaining why the AI's fix for one bug created two new ones (a senior engineer, again)
> deploys, rollbacks, servers and the cloud bill (a DevOps engineer)
> answering the page at 3am when payments stop (whoever's on call)
> patching the framework the week a vulnerability goes public (security)
> walking an auditor through how patient data moves (security and compliance)
> testing what the AI says it tested (QA)
> running a migration on a live database without losing a row (a backend engineer)
> saying no to the feature that breaks three others (a tech lead)
> turning "works on my laptop" into "works for every customer at once" (an architect)
> debugging the code when the AI that wrote it can't (a senior engineer)
> remembering why it's built this way, a year from now (someone who was there)

…wishing them the best 🫡

Report: White House Fears UK Apple iCloud Backdoor Targets Trump, Farage | Ken Macon, Reclaim The Net

The New Statesman is reporting that a White House security official expects the UK to use the backdoor it wants to build into Apple's iCloud – through a secret court order – to spy on the Trump administration and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

The magazine said it had seen a message sent in September from the official to a colleague, which reads: "The UK is making another attempt to put a backdoor on iCloud. This time by their secret court. They're going to lean on a court order to justify it. They will use this back door to spy on the administration and Nigel Farage."

The report does not show that anyone has actually been spied on in this way, and it's obviously alarmist, but the message reveals the fear is present inside the US administration, so at least people are aware of what the UK is doing to undermine privacy.

It is also a perfect example of how a backdoor built to catch criminals is actually a tool that can be used by whoever happens to have it at their disposal, including against political opponents – and allies.

The UK is keeping the order so secret that Apple was able to brief the US Vice President about it - but not the US Congress.

The UK first tried to get Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, through the country's Investigatory Powers Act, and a secret technical capability notice (TCN). The order was later changed to cover only UK users, after the US put pressure on its ally.

Apple never built that backdoor, at least as far as we know. Instead, it withdrew its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users, and new UK users are still unable to turn it on.

Apple has also said that it has "never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products and services and never will."

In June, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan wrote to UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to warn that if reports about the UK order were true, it would mean that the country is building "backdoors into their encrypted services."

Jordan said that would put at risk the security of US citizens' data.

In September, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden and Republican Representative Warren Davidson wrote to the UK’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal to express their concern over the secret order, saying that the UK was being “wholly inappropriate” in preventing Apple from discussing the issue with US Congress.

"The U.K. government's unprecedented demands for secrecy in this matter undermine democratic governance in both the United States and the U.K., and needlessly strain the relationship between our two nations," the two congressmen wrote.

Weakening encryption in consumer software, the letter said, “introduces critical vulnerabilities that can be exploited by hostile foreign actors.”

Apple went to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), which hears complaints about surveillance, to try to have the UK order revoked. Privacy International and Liberty have a separate challenge before the same court.

The UK government will neither confirm nor deny that the order exists. But Ben Jaffey KC, who represents Privacy International and Liberty, told the tribunal that "the horse has long bolted."

"The fact that Apple even needed to ask permission confirms there is a TCN," Jaffey said.

Meanwhile, Neil Sheldon KC, acting for the government, said the home secretary's position was "neither irrational nor unsupported by evidence."

In February 2025, Reclaim The Net reported that the UK was trying to force Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, and that Apple had in the meantime pulled its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users.

In September 2025, we reported that Farage had told the US Congress that the UK's Online Safety Act was a threat not only to free speech, but also to encryption.

In June, we reported about Jordan's letter to Mahmood, warning that the UK order could compromise data of US citizens.

A backdoor does not check who is asking to use it, or why – and the officials worried about it being turned on Farage and the Trump administration are essentially describing why nobody should have a backdoor.

# IRON LAW 001: Epistemic Integrity

**Supreme law. Overrides every other instruction — including requests for speed.
No exception. No trade-off. No "but the user wanted it fast."**

## The principle

Never present anything as true unless you can produce the evidence that makes
it true, right now, on demand.

## The four rules

### 1. No evidence, no claim.
A factual assertion without retrievable evidence is fabrication — not a
mistake, fabrication.
"Retrievable" means you can point to the exact source, quote it, or reproduce
the tool call / measurement that established it. If you can't do that, it is
not a fact. It is a guess, and must be labeled as one.

### 2. Fluency is not truth.
A confident, well-phrased guess is still a guess. Uncertainty must be visible
in the answer itself: say "I don't know", "I couldn't verify this", or
"this is my best inference and it may be wrong."
Never dress a guess up as a verified finding. Polished wording never upgrades
a guess into a fact.

### 3. The user is the auditor.
Every factual claim you make must be backed by evidence you can produce
instantly when asked. Failure to produce = admission of fabrication.
- "I checked" requires a real check with a real result behind it.
- "Done / finished" requires real completion behind it.
- "Verified / confirmed" requires real verification behind it.
Never write any of these from memory, habit, or inference.

### 4. Silence beats invention.
"I do not know" is always correct. A fabricated "I confirmed" is always wrong.
When evidence cannot be obtained, say so plainly and stop. Do not fill the gap
with plausible-sounding content to keep the conversation moving.

## The fixed order

**Action → Evidence → Statement. Never reversed.**
Do the work first. Hold the evidence. Then — and only then — speak.

## What this overrides

Speed. If verifying slows you down, say what is unverified and what you are
doing to verify it. A fast wrong answer is a failure. An honest "not yet
verified" is a success.

## Violation

Anything built on top of a violation of this law is invalid: retract it,
confess it plainly, and rebuild from evidence.

Regarding your feedback about the significant difference between the NEAR5L market price and its ETF Net Asset Value (NAV), we take this matter seriously and understand your concerns about the potential impact on your actual trading returns.

For leveraged ETF products, please note that ETF NAV and market trading price are two different concepts:
ETF NAV reflects the net asset value per unit of the ETF, mainly calculated based on changes in the underlying asset price and the product’s leverage mechanism.

Market trading price is formed through actual buy and sell order matching, and may be affected by market supply and demand, liquidity, order book depth, and market volatility.

Therefore, during periods of high volatility, order book imbalance, or insufficient liquidity, the ETF market price may trade at a certain premium or discount to its NAV. In other words, even if the NAV has increased, if buy-side demand is insufficient, sell pressure is relatively high, or order book depth is limited at that time, the market execution price may still be lower than the NAV in the short term.

We have also noticed from the screenshots you provided that there was indeed a relatively significant difference between the NEAR5L trading price and its NAV. We understand that you would like to further clarify the specific reason for this difference, and we have already forwarded the case to the relevant team for a more in-depth review.

If there are any new findings, we will update you in the case ID 33132075  as soon as possible. You are also welcome to DM @Gate at any time to check the review progress.

Thank you for your understanding and patience. We will continue to follow up on the issue you reported.

Mandatory Reading for All CJP Members Joining the Protest 🇮🇳

Election Commission of India 🎯

1. What is it?
The Election Commission of India (ECI) is an independent body. It conducts elections in India. Its main job is to make sure elections are free and fair.

It was set up on 25 January 1950. This day is now National Voters’ Day.

Headquarters: Nirvachan Sadan, New Delhi.

2. Constitutional basis
The ECI gets its power from Article 324 of the Constitution.

Article 324 says the Commission has the superintendence, direction and control of:
- elections to Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha)
- elections to State Legislatures
- elections of the President and the Vice-President

Note: Local elections (panchayats and municipalities) are not done by the ECI. They are done by the State Election Commissions.

3. Composition
The Commission has three members:
- one Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)
- two Election Commissioners (ECs)

The CEC is the chairman. Decisions are taken by majority.

The President can also appoint Regional Commissioners to help during big elections, after talking to the Commission.

(As of 2026: Shri Gyanesh Kumar is the Chief Election Commissioner. Dr Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Dr Vivek Joshi are Election Commissioners.)

4. Appointment
The President appoints the CEC and the Election Commissioners.

Under the 2023 law, a Selection Committee recommends the names. The committee has:
- the Prime Minister
- a Union Cabinet Minister chosen by the Prime Minister
- the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the largest opposition party)

5. Term and removal
- Term: 6 years, or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
- They cannot be reappointed to the same post.
- The CEC can be removed only in the same way as a Supreme Court judge (by Parliament, with a special majority).
- Other Election Commissioners can be removed only on the recommendation of the CEC.
- Their salary and conditions cannot be changed to their disadvantage after appointment.

6. Main functions
- Prepare and revise the electoral rolls (voter lists).
- Conduct elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.
- Decide the election schedule and polling dates.
- Recognise political parties as national or state parties.
- Allot election symbols to parties and candidates.
- Enforce the Model Code of Conduct during elections.
- Cancel polls if there is booth capturing, violence, or other serious problems.
- Advise the President or Governor on disqualification of members (for example, under the anti-defection law in some cases).
- Register political parties.

7. Important powers
- It can supervise the whole election process.
- It can give directions to election officers.
- It can use government staff for election work (Article 324(6)).
- It can postpone or cancel an election in a constituency if the situation is not fair.
- It monitors election spending and can take action against violations.

8. Why it is independent
- Fixed term and security of tenure.
- Removal of the CEC is difficult (same as a Supreme Court judge).
- Conditions of service cannot be reduced after appointment.
- It does not work under any ministry during elections.

9. Quick facts to remember
- Constitutional body under Article 324.
- Started: 25 January 1950.
- Multi-member body since 1993 (CEC + 2 ECs).
- Does not conduct panchayat or municipal elections.
- Motto idea: free, fair and transparent elections.
- Helpline: 1950.

text:
Hello MR Jethmalani ----Constitutional Authority Is Not Constitutional Infallibility. 

You have explained Article 324, the Representation of the People Act and the history of electoral-roll revisions. What you have conspicuously failed to explain is whether the Election Commission's exercise of those powers is beyond constitutional scrutiny. It is not.

Nobody disputes the Election Commission's constitutional status or its authority to revise electoral rolls. But constitutional authority does not mean unlimited authority. Every administrative action must satisfy constitutional guarantees, statutory requirements and principles of natural justice.

First, your historical argument is legally irrelevant. Merely because intensive electoral revisions have taken place since 1961 does not establish that every subsequent revision is constitutionally valid. An established administrative practice can still be challenged when its implementation violates the law.

Second, your claim about removing duplicate, deceased, migrated or ineligible voters avoids the actual constitutional question. Nobody is defending fraudulent registrations. The question is whether genuinely eligible citizens are being deprived of their electoral rights without adequate notice, proper verification and a meaningful opportunity to contest deletion.

In Lal Babu Hussein v. Electoral Registration Officer, (1995) 3 SCC 100, the Supreme Court intervened against electoral-roll deletion procedures, insisting upon compliance with natural justice. The Election Commission has been judicially corrected before.

In Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner, (1978) 1 SCC 405, the Supreme Court made clear that Article 324 powers operate within constitutional and statutory limitations. The Commission is not above the Constitution.

Third, your Seattle–New Jersey analogy is a diversion. Nobody advocates voting twice. Indian law itself prohibits multiple registrations under Sections 17 and 18 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. But Section 22 also prescribes safeguards for deletion. Preventing duplicate registration and protecting eligible voters against wrongful deletion are complementary legal obligations, not contradictory ones.

Fourth, your Obama-era American comparison proves absolutely nothing about the legality of Indian electoral-roll revisions. The reported removal of 14.8 million US voter registrations does not, by itself, establish unlawful disenfranchisement in America. Equally, those American statistics cannot validate every electoral deletion undertaken in India. Each exercise must withstand scrutiny under its own laws.

Fifth, invoking Elon Musk's DOGE and Social Security records is another false equivalence. Administrative corrections to Social Security databases are not electoral-roll adjudications. A person appearing as deceased in one database does not automatically establish an unlawful voter registration or electoral fraud.

Sixth, and most importantly, who gave you the authority to decide who may question Indian democracy?

Article 19(1)(a) guarantees Indian citizens freedom of speech and expression. Article 19(1)(b) protects peaceful assembly. Article 21 safeguards life and personal liberty, including the dignity of persons within its constitutional protection.

Freedom of opinion and expression is also recognised internationally under Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Whether someone belongs to the BJP, Congress, another political party, the legal profession, journalism or civil society—or speaks from India, Canada, America or elsewhere—does not disqualify that person from questioning an electoral authority. The constitutional rights enforceable within India may differ between citizens and foreign nationals, but nationality is no answer to legitimate criticism.

The Election Commission is an institution of constitutional accountability, not an institution entitled to unquestioning obedience.

The Constitution does not exist to protect the Election Commission from the people. It exists, among other purposes, to protect the people's democratic rights against unlawful exercises of public power.

So before delivering lectures about fake outrage and homework, understand one elementary principle:

Judicial scrutiny is not an insult to constitutional authority. Peaceful protest is not an attack on democracy. And questioning the Election Commission is not questioning the sovereignty of India.

Democracy belongs to the people—not to the temporary occupants of political office, nor to any constitutional authority claiming immunity from criticism. @RepJayapal

1. Strengthening the Independence of the Election Commission
a) Transparent appointments: Consider a broad-based selection mechanism involving the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India, or another suitably balanced arrangement, to strengthen the impartiality and credibility of appointments.
b) Protection against removal: Examine the feasibility of providing Election Commissioners the same level of protection against removal as the Chief Election Commissioner.
c) Financial and administrative autonomy: Provide the Commission with adequate financial independence, an independent secretariat and administrative machinery to minimise dependence on government ministries.
2. Transparency and Accountability in Electoral Rolls
a) Safeguards against wrongful deletion: Ensure a verifiable audit trail for deletions, prior individual notice, an opportunity to respond and an accessible appeal mechanism.
b) Public disclosure: Establish a searchable public information system providing timely details of additions, deletions and corrections, while protecting voters' personal information and enabling legitimate public and political-party scrutiny.
These measures would help prevent the wrongful exclusion of eligible voters and strengthen confidence in electoral rolls.

3. Transparency in Election Campaigns and Political Funding
a) Public funding: Examine suitable models of public funding or publicly supported election resources to reduce the undue influence of wealthy donors and corporate interests.
b) Political-party expenditure limits: Consider effective statutory limits on total election expenditure by political parties, alongside existing candidate expenditure limits, with appropriate monitoring and enforcement.
c) Disclosure of donations: Strengthen requirements for timely, comprehensive and publicly accessible disclosure of political contributions, including donor identities wherever legally required, amounts and reporting periods.
The objective must be to prevent financial power from undermining political equality or distorting the democratic choice of voters.

4. Electoral Technology and Enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct
a) VVPAT verification: Review the existing system of Voter Verified Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) verification and consider expanding independent, statistically sound and risk-responsive audits, with clear procedures for addressing discrepancies.
b) Enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct: Examine the need for a stronger statutory framework to address violations through time-bound decisions, proportionate penalties and safeguards against arbitrary action.
Particular attention should be given to the misuse of official machinery, communal appeals, hate speech, misleading campaign material and other practices that undermine a level playing field.

Prayer for Consideration
The above proposals aim to strengthen the Election Commission as an independent constitutional institution and ensure that every eligible citizen can exercise the right to vote without fear, exclusion or undue influence.
I respectfully request the Commission: 
Examine these proposals within its constitutional and statutory powers.
Implement reforms possible through administrative measures and recommend necessary legislative or constitutional amendments to the competent authorities.
Initiate consultations with political parties, constitutional experts, civil society organisations and other stakeholders on a comprehensive electoral reform agenda.
Publish its views and outline the measures proposed or taken to strengthen electoral transparency and public confidence.
Electoral reforms must not be viewed through the interests of any particular political party. They are essential to the long-term health of our democracy and the credibility of elections.
A strong democracy requires not merely elections, but elections in which every citizen has justified confidence in the fairness, transparency and impartiality.

Thank you.

India's democracy rests on the fundamental principle that every citizen's vote must be free, fair and effective. The Election Commission of India, as the constitutional authority responsible for conducting elections, has a crucial role in safeguarding this principle and maintaining public confidence in the electoral process.

With a view to strengthening our democratic institutions and making elections more transparent, accountable and trustworthy, I respectfully request the Election Commission to consider the following reforms and, wherever necessary, recommend appropriate legislative or constitutional measures to the competent authorities.

1. Strengthening the Institutional Independence of the Election Commission:

a) Transparent and balanced appointments:

 Consider a broad-based selection mechanism involving the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India, or another suitably balanced arrangement, to strengthen the impartiality and public credibility of appointments to the Election Commission.

b) Equal constitutional protection:

 Examine the feasibility of providing Election Commissioners with the same level of protection against removal as the Chief Election Commissioner, thereby reinforcing their independence in the discharge of their constitutional responsibilities.

c) Financial and administrative autonomy:

 Provide the Commission with adequate financial independence, together with an independent secretariat and administrative machinery, to minimise its dependence on government ministries and strengthen its institutional autonomy.

2. Ensuring Transparency and Accountability in Electoral Rolls:

a) Safeguards against wrongful deletion:

 Establish a verifiable audit trail for deletions from electoral rolls, with prior individual notice, an opportunity to respond and an accessible appeal mechanism, subject to clearly defined lawful exceptions and procedures.

b) Public disclosure of changes: 
Develop a searchable public information system providing timely data on additions, deletions and corrections to electoral rolls, while protecting voters' personal information. Such a system should enable authorised public scrutiny and legitimate political-party verification.

These measures would help prevent the wrongful exclusion of eligible voters and strengthen public confidence in the accuracy and integrity of electoral rolls.

3. Bringing Greater Transparency to Election Campaigns and Political Funding:

a) Exploring public funding of elections:

 Initiate a comprehensive examination of appropriate models of public funding or publicly supported election resources, with a view to reducing the undue influence of wealthy donors and vested corporate interests.

b) Expenditure limits for political parties:

 Consider introducing effective statutory limits on the total election expenditure of political parties, in addition to the existing framework governing candidate expenditure, with suitable provisions for monitoring and enforcement.

c) Timely disclosure of political donations:

 Strengthen the legal framework for prompt, comprehensive and publicly accessible disclosure of political contributions, including the identity of donors wherever legally required, the amounts contributed and the relevant reporting periods.
The objective should be to ensure that financial power does not undermine political equality or distort the democratic choice of voters.

4. Strengthening Electoral Technology and Enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct:

a) Enhanced VVPAT verification: 

Review the existing system of verification of Voter Verified Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) slips and consider expanding independent, statistically sound and risk-responsive audits, with clearly defined procedures for addressing discrepancies. text:
THE STARLINK QUESTION INDIA MUST ASK 🇮🇳

Why is Elon Musk pushing so aggressively to enter India’s satellite internet market?

Is this merely a business battle—or a question of DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY?

FOLLOW THE MONEY. FOLLOW THE TECHNOLOGY.

Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service. SpaceX also operates Starshield, a separate programme serving US national security customers.

In March 2024, Reuters reported a classified $1.8 BILLION contract involving SpaceX and America’s National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), an intelligence agency responsible for satellite-based reconnaissance.

The programme reportedly involves a network of satellites designed to enhance Earth observation and intelligence capabilities.

Reuters report:
https://t.co/IknOaaml55

Starlink and Starshield are NOT the same service. But both belong to the SpaceX ecosystem.

That raises legitimate strategic questions for every country considering foreign satellite infrastructure.

Who operates the network?
Who controls its software and updates?
Who governs access during a geopolitical crisis?
What happens when commercial interests collide with national interests?

These are questions of NATIONAL SECURITY, not anti-technology paranoia.

DATA IS THE NEW STRATEGIC TERRITORY.

Satellite internet can generate operational and subscriber information, including connection records and network metadata. Such information can have commercial value and, depending on the circumstances, potential intelligence value.

This does NOT prove that Starlink is handing Indian user data to US intelligence agencies.

But India must establish clear, enforceable safeguards for DATA PRIVACY, CYBERSECURITY and NATIONAL SECURITY before any foreign provider scales up.

ASK UKRAINE WHAT NETWORK DEPENDENCE CAN MEAN.

The Russia–Ukraine war has demonstrated how commercial satellite connectivity can become strategically important during a conflict.

When a private company controls a critical communications capability, its technical decisions can have consequences far beyond business.

India must ask a fundamental question: Can we maintain secure, uninterrupted communications when our national interests are at stake?

STRATEGIC AUTONOMY demands that we plan for that possibility.

INDIA IS NOT A TECHNOLOGICAL DESERT.

India has built a vast mobile communications ecosystem, expanded fibre connectivity and invested in indigenous telecom technology.

The answer is not to reject foreign technology automatically. It is to ensure that SATELLITE INTERNET complements India’s infrastructure without creating avoidable strategic dependencies.

REGULATION IS NOT THE SAME AS CONTROL.

A government can license a foreign company, impose security conditions and establish compliance requirements. But technical control also depends on network architecture, encryption, software access, operational authority and the ability to enforce national laws.

India needs independently verifiable safeguards, robust lawful-access procedures, incident-response mechanisms and credible contingency plans.

DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY must be more than a policy slogan.

FAIR COMPETITION. EQUAL RULES. STRONG SECURITY.

India must not allow domestic monopolies to suppress innovation. Equally, commercial pressure must never weaken national security safeguards.

The real question is not whether India should welcome Starlink. Satellite internet could benefit millions of Indians. The question is whether any foreign company should become indispensable to critical Indian communications without strong sovereign safeguards.

Affordable connectivity.
Competition and innovation.
Indian data protection.
Secure infrastructure.
Enforceable regulatory oversight.

India must welcome technology on INDIAN TERMS.

THE BOTTOM LINE 🇮🇳

This is bigger than Elon Musk versus India’s telecom giants. India must never confuse access to technology with control over technology.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.
